strengths: MaskSub is technically coherent and simple: one shared model learns from an ordinary view using labels and from a heavily masked view using the stop-gradient prediction of the ordinary view. It adds no model parameters, and removing masked ViT tokens limits the reported 50%-mask training overhead to about 1.5x rather than 2x.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. On ImageNet-1k, MaskSub improves DeiT-III ViT-S/B/L/H by 0.3–0.7 points, MAE/BEiT-v2/CLIP fine-tuning by 0.1–0.4, and ResNet/Swin training by 0.1–1.0. The paper also reports gains on ADE20K, COCO, transfer datasets, CLIP pretraining, and every evaluated robustness benchmark.

The authors directly examine computational cost. Under approximately matched GPU-day budgets, MaskSub improves ViT-S/B by 0.5/0.4 points, MAE-fine-tuned ViT-B/L by 0.4/0.6, and ResNet-101/152 by 0.6/0.8. The 400-epoch ViT-B comparison also favors MaskSub over CoSub in both accuracy and measured GPU days.

The ablations are informative: supervising the masked branch with labels instead of distillation yields only 0.1 points versus 0.6 with the proposed loss; performance is stable across 25–75% masking and several loss weights; and the zero-mask, dropout, and drop-path variants help separate masking from generic two-pass self-distillation.

The formulation, pseudocode, default masking ratio, hardware, training recipes, and most implementation details are clearly reported, and code is linked. The manuscript is visually polished and generally easy to follow. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-pcb8ru3f/call-204379f070f64d71ab574169f9025f07/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The principal material limitation is moderate originality. The objective is essentially online weak/strong-view consistency or self-distillation applied to a masked view, closely related to UDA-style consistency and especially CoSub. Using token masking to obtain a more efficient submodel is useful, but the claimed general framework is a relatively incremental conceptual step.

The proposed mechanism is not fully established. Aggregate loss and gradient-norm curves do not demonstrate the asserted sample-wise automatic curriculum, and a teacher can be confidently wrong rather than merely provide an easy target. Per-sample confidence/correctness analysis or controls varying teacher detachment, softness, and quality would be needed to support that causal explanation; the empirical recipe remains valid without it.

Most headline large-scale and downstream results are reported as single values. Repeated-run statistics cover selected 100- and 400-epoch experiments and transfer learning, but not ViT-L/H, the 0.1-point fine-tuning gains, Swin-T, segmentation, detection, or CLIP pretraining. Appendix Table A.13 also states that the DeiT-III baseline comes from the original paper, weakening paired attribution for small margins.

The universal applicability language is stronger than the results. Applying MaskSub during transfer fine-tuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-10/100 accuracy from 99.19/91.89 to 98.82/89.55; the matched-budget ResNet-50 result falls from 80.4 to 80.0; and CLIP fine-tuning has the same best-epoch performance as its baseline. These exceptions should constrain claims about consistent gains across all cases.

Some comparisons do not isolate the method cleanly: the self-distillation table mixes MaskSub with the stronger RSB recipe while several competitors use older baselines, and heterogeneous CLIP-based methods are compared as if directly commensurate. Presentation-only issues include the duplicated CIFAR-100 heading in Table 7, ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16 inconsistencies, and occasional overstated or imprecise wording.

strengths: The shared-weight formulation is technically coherent and exceptionally simple: the clean branch receives supervised loss, while a strongly masked branch matches stop-gradient clean predictions, adding no parameters and little implementation complexity.

The evaluation is unusually broad. MaskSub improves ImageNet training across ViT-S/B/L/H, ResNet, and Swin; multiple pretrained-model fine-tuning recipes; transfer, segmentation, detection, and robustness benchmarks; and even CLIP and BERT settings.

The paper explicitly considers computational cost. MAE-style token removal limits MaskSub to roughly 1.5× baseline computation, and measured equal-budget comparisons generally favor MaskSub over longer training and competing two-pass methods.

Ablations support important design choices: soft distillation targets substantially outperform direct supervision of the masked branch, results are robust across masking ratios and loss weights, and three-run experiments show clear gains in the principal 100- and 400-epoch ViT settings.
The method, pseudocode, training recipes, hardware information, and released-code link make the work clear and reasonably reproducible.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is incremental: MaskSub is fundamentally shared-weight weak-to-strong consistency/self-distillation with masking, closely related to semi-supervised consistency training and CoSub. Its main contribution is demonstrating that this combination works broadly in supervised training rather than introducing a substantially new learning principle.

The masking-specific causal claim is not fully isolated. In Table A.7, a 0%-mask two-branch configuration already improves the 100-epoch baseline from 77.4 to 78.4, while masking raises it further to about 79.2–79.3. Thus, a considerable portion of the gain may arise from self-distillation, stochastic duplicate passes, or changed gradient scaling; a compute-matched clean-view consistency control is missing.

The claims of stabilized training and automatic difficulty control are stronger than the evidence. The convergence plots show improved losses and accuracy, but no divergence frequency, seed variability, or formal stability measure; increasing sub-branch gradient magnitude alone does not establish the proposed mechanism, and softer targets naturally alter loss and gradient scales.

Many headline gains outside the central ablations are only 0.1–0.4 percentage points and are reported without repeated runs or uncertainty, including BEiT-v2 fine-tuning, Swin-T, and several downstream results. Consistency across settings is encouraging, but statistical reliability is unclear for these cases.

Several claimed superiority comparisons are not controlled: the self-distillation and CLIP-based tables mix different base recipes or pretraining procedures, so they cannot attribute absolute state-of-the-art differences to MaskSub. Moreover, the equal-budget ResNet-50 result is 0.4 points below longer baseline training, qualifying the broad efficiency claim.

Presentation refinements include occasionally overstated language, the duplicated “CIFAR100” heading where one column appears to be CIFAR-10, inconsistent ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16 naming, and imprecise use of “sub-branch” for cases where the full network still executes. These do not materially undermine the contribution.

strengths: The manuscript presents a technically coherent and unusually simple method: a clean supervised branch supplies stop-gradient soft targets to a heavily masked branch sharing the same parameters. The equations and pseudocode make the central objective understandable, and the method adds no parameters or inference-time cost. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-gh08wtnr/call-e46820d2006645769905b0bc631a5bde/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The main empirical case is strong and broad. MaskSub improves DeiT-III training across ViT-S/B/L/H and both 400- and 800-epoch schedules, transfers to ResNet and Swin, and is evaluated in fine-tuning, segmentation, detection, robustness, CLIP pretraining, and language tasks. Particularly notable results include ViT-B improving from 83.5 to 84.1, ResNet152 from 81.8 to 82.8, and CLIP zero-shot accuracy from 33.5 to 37.6.

The evaluation explicitly considers training cost. At approximately equal GPU-days, 400-epoch MaskSub improves ViT-B from 83.7 to 84.1 relative to a 600-epoch baseline, while token removal limits ViT training overhead to about 1.5x rather than the 2x cost of several two-branch alternatives.

The ablations substantiate important design choices. Removing the distillation target reduces the ViT-B gain from 0.6 to 0.1 points; results are stable across 25–75% masking and several loss weights; and MaskSub outperforms analogous DropSub and PathSub variants. Selected experiments also report three-run means and standard deviations, with the core ViT-B improvement clearly exceeding observed variation.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: the paper supplies code, hardware and GPU-day measurements, detailed recipes, architecture-specific masking strategies, and implementation information for classification, transfer, detection, segmentation, BERT, and CLIP.
weaknesses: The conceptual originality is limited because the method is fundamentally clean-to-corrupted consistency training with online self-distillation, closely related to UDA-style weak/strong consistency and CoSub. More importantly, the 0%-mask ablation already raises accuracy from 77.4 to 78.4, versus 79.2 with 50% masking. Thus, a substantial portion of the gain comes from duplicated stochastic self-distillation rather than masking, but this result is not analyzed and the paper over-attributes improvement to strong masking. Controlled comparisons with generic supervised consistency, an EMA teacher, and other clean-view self-distillation baselines are missing.

Many of the broadest claimed gains are only 0.1–0.4 points and lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates, including BEiT-v2 fine-tuning, Swin, detection, segmentation, large ViTs, GLUE, and several transfer settings. The paper also states that CLIP fine-tuning with MaskSub has the same best-checkpoint accuracy as the baseline, so its reported last-epoch improvement does not support a claim of higher attainable performance.

The paper repeatedly characterizes ordinary masked training as “unstable,” but its curves are smooth and convergent; they instead show worse loss and accuracy. Likewise, one gradient-norm plot is insufficient to establish the broader claims of automatic difficulty control or sample-wise masking applied “exclusively” to successful examples—the method actually masks every example and only changes its soft target.

Some competitive comparisons are not adequately controlled. Table 6 combines MaskSub with the much stronger RSB recipe while several self-distillation competitors use older recipes, and Appendix Table A.13 explicitly takes the baseline from the DeiT-III paper rather than clearly rerunning it in the same environment. These comparisons support practicality less strongly than the direct within-recipe ablations do.

Compute efficiency is not universal. ResNet and Swin require roughly 2x training computation because masked tokens cannot be removed; under equal GPU-days, ResNet50 with MaskSub is 0.4 points worse than the longer baseline, and no equal-budget Swin comparison is given. This materially qualifies claims that MaskSub is generally a more efficient training solution.

Presentation-only issues include the duplicated “CIFAR100” header in Table 7, inconsistent ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16 naming, several grammatical errors, and occasional overstatements such as “state-of-the-art” based on comparisons that differ in recipe. These are readily correctable and do not determine the recommendation.

strengths: The method is technically simple and sound: a clean branch receives label supervision, while a parameter-sharing masked branch learns from detached clean predictions. It adds no model parameters or inference-time cost, and token removal limits ViT training overhead to roughly 1.5x.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad. Improvements are reported across ViT scales, ResNet, Swin, supervised pretraining, MAE/BEiT/CLIP fine-tuning, transfer learning, ADE20K, COCO, robustness benchmarks, CLIP pretraining, and BERT fine-tuning.

The authors account for training cost rather than relying only on equal-epoch comparisons. At approximately matched GPU budgets, MaskSub obtains 81.2 versus 80.7 for ViT-S and 84.1 versus 83.7 for ViT-B; robustness also improves consistently across every reported distribution shift.

Ablations substantiate important design choices. Replacing distillation yields only 0.1-point gains versus 0.6–0.7 with it, performance is stable over 25–75% masking, and selected ImageNet experiments include three-run means and standard deviations.

The manuscript provides useful implementation detail, including concise pseudocode, model-specific recipes, masking strategies for hierarchical architectures, hardware and GPU-day measurements, and a code URL.
weaknesses: Material: the conceptual novelty is limited and insufficiently distinguished from established weak-to-strong consistency regularization. Equation 3 is effectively consistency/self-distillation between clean and strongly corrupted views; describing UDA's consistency loss as categorically different from distillation does not resolve this close mathematical relationship. More controlled comparisons to such methods are needed to support the originality claims.

Material: statistical evidence is incomplete relative to the size of many gains. Improvements of 0.1–0.4 points for BEiT, Swin, segmentation, detection, and several transfer settings are reported without repeated runs; three-run statistics cover only selected experiments. Some transfer improvements are smaller than the reported standard deviations, contrary to the manuscript's broad significance wording.

Material: the proposed explanation of “automatic difficulty control” is not convincingly established. A small early sub-branch gradient follows mechanically from a near-uniform online teacher, and the single gradient-norm plot does not show that supervision tracks sample correctness or causes the final gain. Confidence/correctness analyses or teacher-temperature and schedule controls are absent.

Material: training overhead remains substantial—about 45–50% for token-dropping ViTs and 2x for ResNet, Swin, DropSub, and PathSub. Equal-budget evidence covers only part of the study, and the ResNet comparison changes both recipe and epoch count (RSB A1 versus A2), weakening causal attribution.

Several comparisons overstate the evidence: the self-distillation table mixes different base recipes, the pretraining table mixes training lengths, and GradAug is trained for 200 epochs while other methods use 400. These results demonstrate favorable tradeoffs but do not always establish direct superiority under controlled conditions.

Presentation/reproducibility refinements remain: Table 7 duplicates the CIFAR100 heading where the first column is CIFAR10, some claims say “all” or “state-of-the-art” despite CIFAR degradation and a tied best CLIP fine-tuning result, and the BERT/CLIP experiments omit seed statistics and several exact configuration or code-version details. These issues should be corrected but do not outweigh the broad, practically useful evidence.

strengths: MaskSub is technically simple and well specified: it combines ordinary supervised loss on the full input with a stop-gradient soft-target loss on a strongly masked view. It adds no parameters or inference-time cost and uses a fixed 50% mask ratio in nearly all vision experiments.

The core ImageNet evidence is strong and consistent. Across ViT-S/B/L/H, MaskSub improves DeiT-III by 0.3–0.7 points at both 400 and 800 epochs; it also improves ResNet, Swin, MAE/BEiT/CLIP fine-tuning, transfer learning, semantic segmentation, detection, and numerous robustness benchmarks.

The paper directly addresses training cost. Compute-matched comparisons show 400-epoch MaskSub outperforming 600-epoch standard training for ViT-B and the larger ResNets, while its ViT implementation costs about 1.5x rather than the 2x cost of several two-branch alternatives.

Ablations substantiate the proposed design: replacing the distillation target with the ground-truth label yields only 0.1-point gains versus 0.6–0.7 with KD; mask-ratio, loss-weight, branch-count, and alternative drop-regularization studies further isolate relevant choices.

Three-seed results support several central ViT and regularization findings, and robustness gains are unusually consistent across ImageNet-V2, ImageNet-A/R/C, ObjectNet, and three spurious-correlation tests.
Pseudocode, detailed training recipes, hardware and GPU-day accounting, and released code make the main experiments reasonably reproducible.
weaknesses: The conceptual originality is moderate. The objective is closely related to established weak-to-strong consistency or self-training: a prediction on an uncorrupted view supervises a strongly augmented view with stop-gradient. The manuscript's claimed distinction between UDA-style “consistency” and its “distillation” loss is not mathematically persuasive; the main novelty is the effective use of heavy token masking in this framework.

Uncertainty reporting is incomplete. Many reported improvements are only 0.1–0.4 points, yet repeated-run statistics are absent for the 800-epoch and large-model results, Swin and ResNet experiments, fine-tuning results, dense prediction, GLUE, CLIP pretraining, and robustness tests. The three-seed studies support the main 400-epoch ViT result but not the full breadth of the claims.

The claim of uniformly broad applicability is overstated. Applying MaskSub during CIFAR-100 fine-tuning reduces ViT-B accuracy from 91.9 to 89.6, and the compute-matched ResNet-50 experiment decreases accuracy from 80.4 to 80.0. These are meaningful counterexamples to the claimed across-the-board benefit.

Training overhead remains material: approximately 1.5x for token-dropping ViTs and 2x for ResNet, Swin, DropSub, and PathSub. The compute-matched results are favorable overall, but not uniformly so, and the method therefore is not a cost-free training-recipe addition.

The “automatic difficulty control” explanation is supported mainly by descriptive loss and gradient curves from one 100-epoch setting. It is plausible, but comparisons against alternatives such as an EMA teacher, target-temperature schedules, or other matched weak/strong consistency objectives are missing, so the proposed mechanism is not uniquely established.

The GLUE and CLIP extensions are promising but comparatively under-supported: GLUE omits task-specific optimization details and variance, while CLIP is evaluated with one model scale and one zero-shot benchmark without repeated runs. They demonstrate feasibility more clearly than general cross-domain effectiveness.

strengths: The method is simple and technically coherent: a shared-weight, masked sub-branch learns from detached full-input predictions while the main branch retains ordinary supervision. It adds no model parameters or inference cost, and token removal limits plain-ViT training cost to about 1.5×.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad: ImageNet training and fine-tuning, multiple ViT scales, ResNet and Swin, transfer datasets, ADE20K, COCO, robustness benchmarks, CLIP, and BERT. Improvements are generally consistent rather than confined to one architecture or benchmark.

Compute-aware comparisons provide meaningful evidence of usefulness. For example, ViT-B with MaskSub reaches 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for a longer 26-GPU-day baseline, and it compares favorably with DataAug, GradAug, and CoSub.

Ablations support important design choices: replacing distillation with hard-label supervision largely removes the gain; performance is robust across masking ratios and several loss weights; and masking outperforms the proposed dropout and drop-path variants.

The algorithm is easy to implement, the appendix reports detailed training recipes, and the manuscript supplies a public code link. These factors make reproduction more plausible despite the scale of the headline experiments.
weaknesses: Material: conceptual originality is modest. The objective is essentially same-model online distillation or consistency regularization between clean and strongly augmented views. Its distinction from generic consistency training and the closely related CoSub framework is more an augmentation and efficiency choice than a fundamentally new learning principle.

Material: the experiments do not fully isolate the benefit of masking from generic self-distillation. In Table A.7, a 0%-mask sub-branch already improves the 100-epoch baseline from 77.4% to 78.4%, whereas 50% masking reaches 79.2%. Thus, a substantial portion of the gain exists without masking, and there is no compute-matched unmasked-consistency control.

Material: uncertainty is missing for many headline results whose gains are only 0.1–0.4 points, including most 800-epoch, fine-tuning, hierarchical-backbone, dense-prediction, robustness, GLUE, and CLIP experiments. Three-run statistics are confined to selected studies, and some baseline statistics are taken from the original DeiT-III paper rather than paired reruns.

Material: several comparisons overstate the evidence. Table 6 places MaskSub on the strong RSB recipe against older methods using weaker recipes; Table 2 says MaskSub outperforms CoSub although their 800-epoch accuracies tie for ViT-B/L/H; and the equal-budget ResNet comparison changes from RSB-A1 to RSB-A2, with MaskSub actually losing 0.4 points for ResNet-50.

Material: the proposed mechanism is not established by the analysis. Increasing sub-branch gradient norms are compatible with the stated intuition but do not demonstrate sample-wise automatic difficulty control or causal stabilization. Masking is applied to every sample, contrary to the claim that it is effectively applied exclusively to successfully predicted samples.

Some breadth claims need qualification. CLIP fine-tuning improves the last-epoch value but not the best attained accuracy; dense-prediction experiments only compare ImageNet-pretrained backbones rather than applying MaskSub during task training; and robustness improvements are not separated from the accompanying increase in ImageNet accuracy.

The favorable 1.5× training cost applies only when masked tokens can be removed in plain ViTs. ResNet and Swin experiments require approximately 2× training compute, limiting the claimed general practicality.

Presentation refinements are needed: the manuscript contains recurrent grammatical errors, inconsistent model names, an unexplained table marker, a duplicated CIFAR-100 heading that should apparently be CIFAR-10, and a computation statement claiming nearly 300% extra cost where the corresponding main-paper table reports 129%.

strengths: The core method is technically coherent, simple, and practical: a shared-weight model learns from ordinary labels on the full image and from stopped-gradient soft targets on a strongly masked view. It adds no model parameters, and MAE-style token removal limits ViT training overhead. The formulation and pseudocode are easy to understand in the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-btk6fo4p/call-9c8d72f705764695946dbb6496894da3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad. MaskSub improves DeiT-III across ViT-S/B/L/H and both 400- and 800-epoch schedules, several pretrained-model finetuning recipes, ResNet and Swin, transfer learning, segmentation, detection, robustness benchmarks, CLIP pretraining, and BERT finetuning. The consistency across substantially different architectures and settings supports practical generality.

The paper explicitly considers computational cost. For example, ViT-B MaskSub reaches 84.1% in 25 V100 GPU-days versus 83.7% for a longer baseline using 26 GPU-days, while 400-epoch ViT-H MaskSub reaches 85.7% compared with 85.2% for the 800-epoch baseline. Actual GPU-day measurements make the usefulness argument more credible than accuracy-only comparisons would.

The ablations establish that soft-target distillation is important: removing it yields only +0.1 points, compared with +0.6 to +0.7 using it. Mask ratio, loss weighting, multiple branches, and dropout/drop-path variants are also examined. Recipe tables, hardware information, selected three-seed results, and released code provide a reasonably strong reproducibility foundation for the principal image-classification experiments.
weaknesses: The principal originality is incremental. The objective is essentially asymmetric consistency/self-distillation between clean and strongly corrupted views, closely related to the weak/strong-view construction of UDA and the two-pass shared-network training of CoSub. The practical choice of token masking and its computational savings are valuable, but the manuscript does not convincingly identify a fundamentally new learning principle relative to these precedents.

The experiments do not fully isolate the source of improvement. In Table A.7, a 0%-mask two-pass distillation configuration already improves the 100-epoch baseline from 77.4% to 78.4%, while 50% masking reaches 79.2%. Thus, a substantial portion of the gain comes from generic second-pass self-distillation or stochastic consistency rather than masking. A matched-compute comparison against unmasked distillation and other strong-view corruptions is needed before concluding that strong masking itself is the essential ingredient.

Uncertainty is reported only for selected experiments. Many headline improvements in finetuning are 0.1–0.4 points, while the 800-epoch large-model, robustness, CLIP-pretraining, GLUE, detection, and segmentation results appear to be single runs. This is especially consequential for high-variance settings such as GLUE. Moreover, Table A.10's claim that transfer gains exceed standard deviations is not generally true; several gains are smaller than the reported deviations.

The efficiency advantage is architecture-dependent. MaskSub adds about 45% training time for token-dropping ViTs but approximately doubles training cost for ResNet and Swin. Under the matched-budget comparison in Table A.1, ResNet-50 MaskSub is worse than the longer baseline, 80.0% versus 80.4%. The paper should therefore qualify its broad efficiency claims.

The proposed mechanism of “automatic difficulty control” is supported only by aggregate gradient norms in one ViT-B setting. A near-uniform early teacher naturally produces small distillation gradients, which does not establish the stronger claim that masking is applied effectively only to successfully classified samples. There is no per-sample confidence/correctness analysis, and confidently wrong teacher predictions remain possible.

Minor clarity and reproducibility issues remain: the loss equations omit an explicit sum over classes; Table 7 labels both CIFAR columns as CIFAR100; ViT-H is inconsistently called /14 and /16; and the GLUE and CLIP experiments omit important hyperparameters, software versions, seed statistics, and dataset-mixture details. These are presentation or reporting refinements rather than reasons by themselves to reject the work.

strengths: MaskSub is technically coherent, simple, and practically attractive: a clean supervised pass supplies detached soft targets to a strongly masked pass through the same network, adding no inference-time parameters. The formulation and pseudocode are easy to understand. Source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-arr_ufzx/call-29e3ace1e70247c8aac0ee6f56b12e56/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical breadth is unusually strong. MaskSub improves 400- and 800-epoch DeiT-III results across ViT-S through ViT-H by 0.3–0.7 points, and gains also appear for MAE, BEiTv2, and CLIP fine-tuning, ResNet, Swin, semantic segmentation, detection, transfer learning, and numerous robustness benchmarks.

The compute-aware evidence is valuable. For example, ViT-B MaskSub reaches 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for a longer baseline in 26 GPU-days, and it outperforms DataAug, GradAug, and CoSub in the reported 400-epoch comparison while requiring less additional computation.

The ablations support important design choices: replacing the distillation target with labels reduces gains to about 0.1 points, several masking ratios work, the method is insensitive across a reasonable range of loss weights, and masking performs better than dropout or drop-path variants. Three-run results for the principal 400-epoch ViT-S/B experiments and the shorter analyses generally place the improvements beyond the reported variation.

The manuscript provides useful implementation information, including training recipes, hardware and GPU-day measurements, masking choices for different architectures, and released code. The fixed 50% ratio across the main vision experiments further improves usability.
weaknesses: The main originality and causal-attribution concern is that the method closely resembles established weak/strong-view consistency training and online self-distillation. Crucially, the 0%-mask two-pass variant already improves the 100-epoch baseline from 77.4% to 78.4%, while 50% masking reaches 79.2%. Thus, a substantial portion of the gain does not require masking. A matched clean-view distillation control and stronger comparisons to supervised consistency methods are needed to isolate the claimed masking-specific contribution.

Most headline results are single runs despite several gains being only 0.1–0.4 points, including BEiTv2, Swin-T, COCO, and average BERT-large GLUE results. The replicated ViT-S/B experiments are reassuring, but they do not establish the significance of the numerous small gains used to support broad generality; some individual GLUE and CIFAR results also regress.

Training efficiency is architecture-dependent. Token removal makes ViT training approximately 1.5 times as expensive per epoch, but ResNet and Swin require roughly twice the training budget. In the sole cost-matched ResNet-50 comparison, MaskSub is 0.4 points worse, and no cost-matched Swin result is supplied. Claims of general computational superiority should therefore be restricted mainly to token-prunable ViTs.

The proposed explanation of “automatic difficulty control” is suggestive rather than established. A gradient-norm trace for one configuration does not demonstrate that this mechanism causes the accuracy gain, and masking is applied to every sample rather than exclusively to correctly predicted samples as the text implies. Teacher entropy/confidence controls or comparisons with scheduled loss weighting would better support this claim.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled: contrasting supervised MaskSub against self-supervised MAE pretraining mixes supervision regimes, while several self-distillation comparisons use different and weaker base recipes. These tables provide context but do not strongly establish superiority over the closest methodological alternatives.

Presentation-level issues are noticeable but not decision-critical: Table 7 labels both CIFAR columns as CIFAR-100, ViT-H/14 is occasionally called ViT-H/16, the claimed universally fixed masking ratio has a stated 15% BERT exception, and details such as BatchNorm-statistics handling for the two ResNet passes could be clearer.

strengths: MaskSub is technically coherent and unusually simple: it combines ordinary supervised learning on an unmasked view with detached clean-view distillation to a masked, weight-sharing view. It adds no parameters or inference-time cost, while token removal limits ViT training cost to about 1.5x rather than two full passes.

The empirical breadth is strong. Table 1 reports gains of 0.3-0.7 points across ViT-S/B/L/H and two training lengths; improvements also appear for MAE, BEiTv2, and CLIP fine-tuning, ResNet and Swin architectures, transfer learning, ADE20K, COCO, robustness benchmarks, GLUE, and CLIP pretraining.

The paper makes a meaningful effort to account for compute. In Table A.1, 400-epoch MaskSub ViT-S/B models outperform 600-epoch baselines at approximately equal GPU-days by 0.5/0.4 points, and the method is cheaper than other two-pass approaches in Tables 9 and A.2.

The ablations support several design choices: removing distillation reduces the 400-epoch gain from 0.6-0.7 to 0.1 points; results are insensitive to masking ratios from 40%-75%; and loss-weight, multiple-branch, dropout, and drop-path variants are examined.

The algorithm, masking variants, training recipes, hardware, downstream protocols, and selected multi-seed results are documented, and public code is reported, making reproduction reasonably feasible. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-q1_j8ej8/call-ac369567aae94fb6981f5300b20ba248/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: Material - originality is limited. The central clean-teacher/strongly-corrupted-student consistency objective is close to prior self-distillation and consistency training, especially CoSub and UDA, while directly relevant precedents such as supervised augmentation-consistency and R-Drop receive insufficient discussion. The efficient use of input masking is a useful specialization, but not an entirely new learning principle.

Material - the evidence does not cleanly isolate masking from generic two-pass consistency. In Table A.7, a 0% masking sub-branch already improves the 100-epoch baseline from 77.4 to 78.4, versus 79.2 with 50% masking. Thus, over half of that observed gain exists without masking, weakening claims that strong masking is the essential source of improvement.

Material - averaging CE and KD halves the direct supervised-loss weight, while the KD gradient is initially small. Consequently, MaskSub also changes the effective gradient or learning-rate schedule. No baseline with matched supervised-gradient scaling or an unmasked consistency branch at the principal 400/800-epoch settings separates this effect. The smooth curves and gradient norms in Figure 2 are descriptive and do not establish the claimed training “instability” or automatic curriculum.

Material - most headline improvements, especially the 0.1-0.4-point fine-tuning, Swin, detection, and segmentation gains, are reported from single runs. Multi-seed results cover only selected settings, and Table A.13 takes its baseline from prior work rather than a paired rerun. GLUE also contains several task regressions, making its small average gain uncertain.

Material - several comparisons do not isolate method quality: Table 6 compares absolute accuracies obtained with substantially different base recipes; Table 4 mixes heterogeneous pretraining methods; and the compute-matched ResNet comparison changes from RSB-A1 to RSB-A2. The appendix additionally shows MaskSub losing by 0.4 points for compute-matched ResNet-50, which is omitted from the main compute table.

The practical tradeoff remains meaningful: MaskSub adds roughly 45%-50% training time for ViTs and about 100% for ResNet/Swin, while many gains are modest. Minor presentation issues, including the duplicated CIFAR-100 header and inconsistent ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16 naming, should also be corrected but are not acceptance-determining.

strengths: The method is technically coherent and unusually simple: a normally supervised full-input pass provides detached soft targets to the same network on a masked input. It adds no model parameters, and MAE-style token removal limits the reported training overhead to roughly 1.5× at 50% masking.

The within-recipe evidence is broad and consistently favorable. MaskSub improves DeiT-III across ViT-S/B/L/H and both 400- and 800-epoch schedules by 0.3–0.7 points, and also improves MAE, BEiT-v2, and CLIP fine-tuning, ResNet, and Swin baselines.

The paper considers computational cost rather than comparing accuracy alone. At approximately equal GPU-days, 400-epoch MaskSub improves over 600-epoch standard training by 0.5 points for ViT-S and 0.4 for ViT-B; the appendix also transparently reports the negative ResNet-50 result.
Transfer, ADE20K segmentation, COCO detection/segmentation, and multiple ImageNet robustness evaluations generally improve, supporting usefulness beyond ImageNet validation accuracy.

Ablations examine the distillation loss, masking ratio, loss weights, multiple sub-branches, and dropout/drop-path variants. Pseudocode, detailed recipes, hardware costs, partial three-seed results, and a public code link make the work reasonably reproducible.
weaknesses: Material: The conceptual novelty is incremental. The method is essentially one-way consistency/self-distillation between weak and strongly corrupted views, closely related to UDA-style consistency, CoSub, and dual-pass dropout approaches such as R-Drop. The distinctions are primarily the supervised setting, asymmetric loss, and masking implementation; broader direct comparisons are missing.

Material: The mask-specific attribution is incomplete. In Table A.7, a 0%-mask duplicated distillation pass already raises accuracy from 77.4 to 78.4, versus 79.2 at 50% masking. Thus, a substantial portion of the gain may come from dual-pass self-distillation itself; a compute-matched unmasked-distillation baseline and comparisons using other strong corruptions are needed to substantiate the central masking claim.

Material: Many headline improvements are only 0.1–0.4 points, yet repeated-run statistics are provided only for selected experiments. Variance is not reported for the large models, most fine-tuning results, hierarchical architectures, robustness benchmarks, or the large CLIP pretraining gain, limiting confidence in the smallest differences.

Material: Several state-of-the-art comparisons are confounded. Table 6 compares RSB+MaskSub against methods using weaker recipes, Table 4 mixes different pretraining approaches, and the compute-matched ResNet study changes from RSB-A1 to RSB-A2 as well as adding MaskSub. These tables do not isolate the proposed method as cleanly as the paired within-recipe comparisons do.

Material: The claimed “automatic difficulty control” is supported mainly by loss and gradient curves from one ViT-B setting, not a causal ablation. Masking is applied to every sample rather than exclusively to samples with successful main-branch predictions, and confidently incorrect teacher outputs can also supervise the masked branch.

Presentation refinement: The writing repeatedly overstates modest gains and contains avoidable inconsistencies, including the duplicated CIFAR-100 heading in Table 7, ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16, “MaskSup,” duplicated ResNet references, and numerous grammatical errors. These reduce polish but are not acceptance-determining.

strengths: The method is technically coherent and unusually simple: it combines supervised learning on an unmasked view with stop-gradient distillation from that view to a heavily masked view, sharing all parameters and adding no inference-time cost.

The empirical breadth is strong. MaskSub improves DeiT-III across ViT-S/B/L/H by 0.3–0.7 points, ResNets by 0.3–1.0, Swin models by 0.1–0.4, and multiple MAE, BEiT-v2, and CLIP fine-tuning settings. Improvements also extend to segmentation, detection, transfer, and numerous robustness benchmarks.

Compute-aware comparisons support practical usefulness: ViT-B MaskSub reaches 84.1% in 25.1 GPU-days versus 83.7% for a longer baseline in 26 GPU-days and 83.9% for CoSub in 35.3 GPU-days. MAE-style token removal limits the ViT overhead to approximately 45–50%.

The ablations substantiate key design choices. Replacing distillation with hard-label training reduces the gain from 0.6–0.7 to 0.1 points; results are stable across 25–75% masking; loss-weight, branch-count, dropout, and drop-path studies are also provided.

The paper is clear and substantially reproducible through equations, concise pseudocode, training recipes, hardware and GPU-day reporting, and a stated code release. This assessment covers the manuscript and appendix :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-tj17pj6p/call-358bd3a6975348b1b08f7eaab57cbd7d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: Material: the conceptual novelty is moderate. The objective is essentially weak-to-strong consistency or online self-distillation applied to a masked second view; the distinction from UDA-like consistency learning and related two-view schemes is mainly its fully supervised setting, masking choice, and efficient implementation.

Material: uncertainty is not reported for most decisive large-scale results. Many fine-tuning, Swin, detection, and BEiT-v2 gains are only 0.1–0.4 points, while three-run statistics are confined to selected ablations and transfer experiments; some baseline statistics are drawn from the original DeiT-III report rather than a matched rerun.

Material: the claimed stabilization and automatic difficulty-control mechanism is supported primarily by one 100-epoch ViT-B loss/gradient study. Increasing sub-branch gradient magnitude does not uniquely establish that explanation, and comparisons against masking curricula, EMA teachers, temperature-controlled distillation, or symmetric consistency are absent.

Material: efficiency is architecture-dependent. MaskSub doubles training cost for ResNet and Swin because their masked inputs do not permit token removal, and at matched compute the ResNet-50 result is 0.4 points below the longer baseline. Thus, claims of broadly superior compute efficiency are stronger than the evidence supports.

Presentation/evidence: several comparisons are not controlled enough to establish superiority over self-distillation broadly; Table 6 mixes substantially different baseline recipes, and Table 2 mixes objectives and training lengths. Details such as branch-wise augmentation sharing, BatchNorm-statistics handling for ResNets, and applying the objective to GLUE regression tasks are also insufficiently specified.

strengths: MaskSub is technically simple and practical: it combines ordinary supervised learning on an unmasked view with stop-gradient self-distillation on a strongly masked view, shares all parameters, and adds no inference-time model complexity. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xp9x2kgc/call-9e8ba744a6d949c89cd0acf3cbe716d3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical coverage is unusually broad. Improvements are reported across DeiT-III model scales, ResNet and Swin, MAE/BEiT-v2/CLIP fine-tuning, transfer learning, ADE20K, COCO, robustness benchmarks, CLIP pretraining, and BERT fine-tuning.

The paper accounts for its substantial training overhead. For example, the equal-budget comparison reports ViT-B at 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% in 26 GPU-days, and the method's token removal limits ViT training cost to roughly 1.5x rather than 2x.

The ablations cover masking ratio, loss weighting, hard versus distilled targets, multiple sub-branches, and alternative drop regularizers. Selected experiments include three-run means and standard deviations, and the appendix provides recipes, hardware information, and a public code link.
weaknesses: The originality is incremental. The core mechanism is clean-to-corrupted consistency/self-distillation, closely related to UDA-style weak/strong consistency and especially CoSub. The distinctions are primarily the masking corruption and computational benefit; related consistency methods such as R-Drop and AugMix are not adequately situated or compared.

The experiments do not cleanly attribute the gain to strong masking. In Table A.6, masked training with hard labels improves only 0.1 points, whereas adding distillation yields 0.6–0.7. More importantly, Table A.7's 0%-mask two-pass self-distillation already improves ViT-B from 77.4 to 78.4, versus 79.2 at 50% masking. An equal-compute comparison against this no-mask self-distillation control is missing, weakening the claim that masking itself is the principal contribution.

The claimed explanation in terms of training stability and automatic difficulty control is not established. The evidence consists mainly of loss and gradient-norm curves; it does not measure divergence, variance across runs, or gradient conflict. A small early student gradient also follows mechanically from a near-uniform early teacher, and every sample is still masked, contrary to the statement that masking is applied exclusively to successful samples.

Statistical evidence is incomplete for many of the smallest reported gains, including +0.1 on BEiT-v2 and Swin-T and +0.2–0.3 on several downstream tasks. Replicate statistics are supplied only for selected settings, so the broad claim of consistent improvement is stronger than the evidence. Some comparison tables also mix different base recipes, making the self-distillation and state-of-the-art claims less controlled.

Reproducibility is helped by the code and appendix, but the manuscript omits some branch-level implementation details and gives limited settings for GLUE and CLIP pretraining. Minor presentation errors include the duplicated CIFAR100 heading in Table 7 and inconsistent ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16 naming; these are refinements rather than acceptance-determining flaws.

These results support a broad positive trend but do not establish that every small improvement is statistically reliable.

The proposed explanation is under-supported. Aggregate gradient curves are compatible with gradual consistency learning, but they do not demonstrate the claimed sample-wise automatic difficulty control or genuine training instability; no relationship between teacher confidence/correctness and sub-branch gradients is measured. Moreover, shared parameters mean the main model is still affected by sub-branch gradients despite the stopped teacher path.

Some comparisons overstate what can be concluded. Table 6 contrasts MaskSub on the stronger RSB recipe with self-distillation methods using different, often weaker recipes, while Table 4's claimed advantage over other CLIP-based methods is only 0.1 point under non-identical setups. These tables do not establish method-level superiority, although the within-recipe baseline comparisons remain informative.

Reproducibility and scope claims have smaller gaps: branch stochasticity and BatchNorm handling for ResNets, mask/augmentation ordering, and complete GLUE/CLIP schedules are not specified. The assertion of one fixed 50% setting also has exceptions—BERT uses 15%, and hierarchical models require architecture-specific masking and 2× training cost. Table-header errors, ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16 inconsistencies, and several overstated or grammatically unclear claims are presentation refinements rather than rejection-level issues.

strengths: MaskSub is technically coherent and practical: a shared model learns from ground-truth supervision on the unmasked input and detached soft predictions on a masked view. It adds no parameters, and MAE-style token removal limits ViT training cost to roughly 1.5x while leaving inference unchanged.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad. ImageNet gains are consistent across ViT-S/B/L/H at 400 and 800 epochs (+0.3 to +0.7 points), MAE/BEiT-v2/CLIP fine-tuning, ResNet and Swin, transfer learning, ADE20K, COCO, robustness benchmarks, GLUE, and CLIP pretraining; the latter improves zero-shot accuracy from 33.5 to 37.6.

The paper treats compute as a first-class concern. Equal-GPU-day comparisons show, for example, ViT-B MaskSub reaching 84.1 in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7 for a longer 26-GPU-day baseline, and MaskSub has a better accuracy-cost tradeoff than the reported DataAug, GradAug, and CoSub alternatives.

The ablations provide useful support: replacing distillation with ordinary masked-label training reduces gains to about +0.1 versus +0.6–0.7; performance is stable over 40–75% masking; loss weights, multiple branches, other augmentations, dropout, and drop-path are examined. Three-run statistics are also supplied for several central experiments.

The presentation is generally clear, with concise pseudocode, detailed training recipes, hardware and GPU-day reporting, masking implementations for different architectures, and a public code link, making the core method reasonably reproducible.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. The method instantiates the established weak/strong-view consistency or self-distillation pattern using an unmasked teacher view and masked student view, making it particularly close to UDA-style consistency and CoSub. The paper explains these distinctions but does not provide a tightly controlled comparison against a strong same-recipe generic consistency/self-distillation baseline.

The evidence does not fully isolate masking as the source of improvement. In Table A.7, a 0%-mask second branch already raises the 100-epoch result from 77.4 to 78.4, while 50% masking reaches 79.2. Comparable full-view self-distillation controls are absent from the headline 400/800-epoch settings, so a substantial portion of the gain may come from the second-pass self-distillation objective rather than masking. Likewise, the single gradient-norm study is correlational and does not by itself establish the claimed automatic difficulty-control mechanism.

Many headline improvements are only 0.1–0.4 points and are reported from single runs. Three-seed results are limited to selected 100/400-epoch and transfer experiments, excluding the 800-epoch large models, most fine-tuning results, ResNet/Swin, downstream tasks, GLUE, and CLIP. Some transfer improvements are also smaller than the reported standard deviations, so claims of consistent or statistically meaningful gains are too broad.

The practical advantage carries meaningful training overhead: approximately 1.5x for token-dropping ViTs and 2x for ResNet/Swin. Equal-budget ViT comparisons are helpful, but the ResNet comparison changes from RSB-A1 to RSB-A2 as well as changing epochs, and several literature comparisons mix recipes or omit costs, limiting clean attribution and fairness.

Some generality and reproducibility statements need qualification. Applying MaskSub during transfer fine-tuning substantially hurts CIFAR-10/100 in Table 7, and BERT uses 15% masking despite the claim that 50% is used across all experiments. Exact batch-normalization handling for masked ResNet passes, the bidirectional CLIP distillation loss, and GLUE task-specific settings are underspecified. Minor presentation errors include the duplicated CIFAR100 heading, ViT-H/16 versus ViT-H/14 inconsistency, and inconsistent prose about GradAug cost.

strengths: The method is simple and technically coherent: it combines supervised loss on an unmasked view with stop-gradient self-distillation to a strongly masked view, adds no parameters, and can reduce the masked branch's cost by removing tokens.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad. ImageNet gains are consistent across ViT-S/B/L/H at 400 and 800 epochs (+0.3 to +0.7 points), as well as ResNet, Swin, pretrained-model fine-tuning, transfer learning, ADE20K segmentation, COCO detection, robustness benchmarks, BERT, and CLIP pretraining.

Compute-aware comparisons strengthen the practical case. For example, ViT-B with MaskSub reaches 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for a longer 26-GPU-day baseline, and it is more efficient than the evaluated DataAug, GradAug, and CoSub alternatives.

The ablations cover the essential components. Removing distillation reduces the 400-epoch gain to +0.1 versus +0.6/+0.7 with distillation; mask ratios, loss weights, multiple branches, and dropout/drop-path variants are also examined. Selected experiments include three-seed means and deviations.
The core vision experiments are reasonably reproducible from the pseudocode, released-code link, detailed training recipes, hardware information, and measured GPU costs.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is modest. Equation (3) is essentially one-way weak/strong-view consistency or self-distillation, closely related to UDA-style training, CoSub, and self-distillation with dropout. The primary novelty is the masked student construction and its extensive validation rather than a new learning principle.

The claimed mechanism of "automatic difficulty control" is not established by the aggregate gradient-norm curve. Masking is applied to every sample, and no analysis conditions gradients on teacher correctness, confidence, or target entropy. Moreover, the zero-mask self-distillation control already improves the 100-epoch baseline from 77.4% to 78.4%, versus 79.2% at 50% masking, so a substantial fraction of the gain is not specific to masking.

Several headline improvements are small and lack uncertainty estimates, including +0.1 for BEiTv2 and Swin-T and +0.2/+0.3 for COCO. The paper also states that CLIP fine-tuning has the same best accuracy with and without MaskSub; its reported +0.4 gain comes only from comparing the last epoch, weakening the associated capability claim.

MaskSub has meaningful overhead: approximately 1.5× per epoch for token-dropping ViTs and 2× for hierarchical architectures. Although compute-matched results are generally favorable, they are not uniformly so—ResNet-50 is 0.4 points worse in the appendix—and Table 2 omits comparable compute figures for MAE and SupMAE despite making efficiency-oriented comparisons.

The beyond-vision evidence is less reproducible and conclusive than the core experiments: GLUE lacks task-specific optimization details, seed variation, and an explanation of the distillation loss for STS-B regression, while CLIP pretraining is evaluated with one model and data mixture without variance or compute reporting. As a presentation-only issue, Table 7 incorrectly labels both CIFAR columns as CIFAR-100, and terms such as "state-of-the-art" and "substantial advancement" overstate some tied or marginal results.

strengths: MaskSub is technically simple and plausible: a full-image branch receives label supervision while a shared-weight masked branch matches detached full-image predictions. It adds no parameters or inference cost, and token removal limits ViT-B/400 training overhead to a measured 45% (25.1 versus 17.3 GPU-days).

The central ImageNet evidence is consistent across scale: DeiT-III gains are 0.6–0.7 points at 400 epochs and 0.3–0.5 at 800 epochs for ViT-S/B/L/H. Reported three-run results for 400-epoch ViT-S/B support gains beyond run variance, including 84.08±0.02 versus 83.46±0.04 for ViT-B.

Evaluation breadth is unusually strong. Results cover ResNet, Swin, pretrained-model fine-tuning, transfer learning, segmentation, detection, robustness, CLIP pretraining, and BERT. Robustness improvements are especially meaningful; for example, ViT-B improves from 36.8 to 41.9 on ImageNet-A while ImageNet-C error decreases from 38.1 to 36.9.

The ablations substantiate important design choices: replacing distillation with hard-label supervision reduces the ViT-B gain from 0.6 to 0.1 points, performance is robust across 25–75% masking, and loss-weight and multi-branch alternatives are examined. Equal-GPU-day comparisons also generally favor MaskSub over merely extending training.

The paper is readable and practically oriented, with equations, concise pseudocode, detailed recipe tables, hardware costs, and a code link. This combination makes the method potentially useful as a low-complexity training plug-in.
weaknesses: The masking-specific contribution is not fully isolated from generic online consistency/self-distillation and optimization changes. In Table A.7, a 0%-mask version already raises accuracy from 77.4 to 78.4, while 50% masking reaches 79.2. Thus, a substantial fraction of the improvement arises without masking. Missing controls include a second unmasked stochastic pass and a CE-only baseline with the same one-half loss scaling or corresponding learning-rate change.

The claimed mechanism is stronger than the evidence. Lower training losses and evolving gradient norms show compatible behavior but do not establish “training instability” or a causal automatic curriculum; there are no divergence/variance measures or comparisons with explicit masking schedules, delayed consistency, or alternative teacher constructions. Masking is also applied to every sample, so describing it as exclusively applied to successfully predicted images is imprecise.

Uncertainty is reported only for selected experiments. Several conclusions rely on small single-run differences—0.1 for BEiT-v2 and Swin-T, 0.2–0.3 for MAE and COCO, and 0.4–0.6 for segmentation—without confidence intervals. The BERT results include task-level regressions, and neither BERT nor CLIP results include repeated-run statistics, weakening the strongest generality claims.

The compute-matched evidence is favorable but not conclusive. Longer baselines appear to reuse schedules without demonstrated retuning, and the ResNet comparison changes from RSB-A1 for the 600-epoch baseline to RSB-A2 for MaskSub. The omitted ResNet-50 case in the main compute table actually favors the baseline by 0.4 points in Appendix Table A.1, so compute superiority is not universal.

Novelty relative to clean/strong-view consistency learning, UDA-style training, CoSub, and masked distillation is modest and primarily empirical; the related-work discussion does not provide sufficiently controlled comparisons to distinguish these formulations. Minor, correctable presentation issues include underspecified BCE/CLIP objectives, ambiguous hierarchical masking details, a duplicated CIFAR-100 heading in Table 7, and inconsistent ViT-H /14 versus /16 labels.

strengths: The method is simple and technically plausible: an unmasked supervised pass supplies detached soft targets to a strongly masked pass through the same network. It adds no parameters or inference cost, and MAE-style token removal limits ViT training cost to about 1.5×. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-0h7_zclx/call-87c06b8826ab48aa8165e525b27348b8/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical breadth is unusually strong. MaskSub improves 400- and 800-epoch DeiT-III training across ViT-S/B/L/H by 0.3–0.7 points, and also improves ResNet, Swin, MAE/BEiT/CLIP fine-tuning, transfer learning, segmentation, detection, and numerous robustness benchmarks.

The evaluation considers training cost rather than only accuracy. For example, ViT-B MaskSub obtains 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for a longer baseline in 26 GPU-days; analogous controlled-budget gains are reported for ViT-S and larger ResNets.

Useful ablations support the design: replacing distillation with ground-truth supervision reduces the 400-epoch gain from 0.6–0.7 to 0.1 points; mask-ratio and loss-weight sweeps are provided; and selected experiments report three-run means and standard deviations. Equations, pseudocode, detailed recipes, hardware information, and a code link aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The conceptual originality is moderate. The core construction is weak-to-strong consistency/self-distillation with masking and shared weights. The paper explains distinctions from UDA and CoSub, but controlled comparisons cover only a narrow subset of closely related consistency and self-distillation alternatives, while several headline comparisons use results from different recipes or papers.

Statistical support is incomplete for the many small gains. Most costly experiments report only one value, including several 0.1–0.4-point fine-tuning and downstream improvements. Moreover, Table A.13 states that the DeiT-III baseline is taken from the original paper, making it unclear whether all claimed improvements reflect paired runs under identical implementations and seeds.

The proposed “automatic difficulty control” explanation is suggestive rather than established: the gradient-norm curves show correlation but do not isolate teacher entropy or confidence as the cause. Notably, the 0%-mask two-pass control already improves 100-epoch accuracy from 77.4 to 78.4, so a substantial component can arise from duplicate stochastic self-distillation rather than strong masking itself; this deserves clearer analysis and interpretation.

Some comparative claims are overstated. The self-distillation table changes both recipe and sometimes architecture across methods, and the CLIP-based comparison mixes pretraining approaches. Equal-budget MaskSub also underperforms the longer ResNet-50 baseline by 0.4 points in Table A.1, so compute efficiency is not universal.

Minor presentation issues include the duplicated CIFAR-100 header where the first column is evidently CIFAR-10, imprecise use of “sub-branch” for a shared full network receiving fewer tokens, and the statement that GradAug adds almost 300% cost although Table 9 reports 129% additional cost. These do not undermine the main result but reduce clarity.

strengths: The method is technically coherent and simple: clean-view predictions supervise a strongly masked, shared-weight branch through detached soft targets, adding no parameters or inference overhead. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-reialsei/call-98d7bdb557c94e9b97954f38b2eb9e6f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Evidence is unusually broad. MaskSub improves DeiT-III across four ViT sizes and two training lengths by 0.3–0.7 points, and also benefits MAE/BEiT-v2/CLIP fine-tuning, ResNet, Swin, GLUE, and CLIP pretraining.

The evaluation extends beyond ImageNet accuracy to transfer learning, ADE20K segmentation, COCO detection/instance segmentation, and numerous robustness benchmarks; the consistent robustness gains are particularly compelling.
Compute-aware comparisons show that token removal limits ViT training overhead to roughly 1.5× and that MaskSub generally outperforms longer baseline training at comparable GPU-day budgets.

Ablations cover KD targets, masking ratios, loss weights, multiple branches, alternative drop regularizers, and selected three-seed experiments. The method is insensitive across 40–75% masking, supporting practical usability.
Detailed recipe tables, reported hardware costs, concise pseudocode, and a public code link provide a reasonably strong basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: Material: originality is moderate. The core is clean/strong-view consistency training with online self-distillation, closely related to UDA-style consistency and CoSub. The manuscript explains procedural differences but does not establish a strong conceptual distinction from these precedents.

Material: the claimed importance of masking is incompletely isolated. At 100 epochs, a 0%-mask sub-branch already raises accuracy from 77.4 to 78.4, versus 79.2 at 50% masking, while removing KD reduces the long-schedule gain to only 0.1 points. Thus, much of the benefit may arise from self-distillation, stochastic dual passes, or changed gradient scaling; a long-schedule clean-view self-distillation control is missing.

Material: most headline and cross-domain results are single runs, including many gains of only 0.1–0.4 points. Three-seed statistics are restricted mainly to short analyses, transfer experiments, and 400-epoch ViT-S/B; some baselines are imported from prior work rather than paired reruns. Consequently, the smallest reported gains are not convincingly above run-to-run variation.

The claimed “training stability” and “automatic difficulty control” are stronger than the evidence. Loss and gradient-norm trajectories show improved convergence and an increasing sub-branch gradient, but no instability metric, failure-rate analysis, uncertainty bands, teacher-entropy analysis, or causal comparison against an explicit curriculum is provided.

Efficiency conclusions need qualification: hierarchical models require approximately 2× training compute, the cost-matched ResNet-50 result is 0.4 points below its comparator, and some cost comparisons change both recipe and epoch count. MaskSub often matches rather than exceeds CoSub accuracy, with its clearer advantage being lower compute.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete for exact mask placement, handling of stochastic layers and BatchNorm during sequential branch passes, the BCE/mixup formulation, and both directions of the CLIP contrastive objective.

Presentation issues are minor but recurrent: duplicated CIFAR-100 headers where one should be CIFAR-10, inconsistent ViT-H suffixes, several typographical errors, and occasional overstatements such as calling small unreplicated gains “remarkable.”

strengths: The method is technically sound and simple: a clean, label-supervised pass supplies detached soft targets to a strongly masked pass through the same network. It adds no inference parameters or inference cost, while token removal limits ViT training overhead to roughly 45–50%. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-hivkqagz/call-1435d14317fd4fbab4ced10418e34ff7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical coverage is unusually broad. MaskSub improves DeiT-III training across ViT-S/B/L/H by 0.3–0.7 points, multiple pretrained-model fine-tuning recipes by 0.1–0.4, and ResNet/Swin training by 0.1–1.0; downstream segmentation, detection, transfer, and robustness results generally agree with the ImageNet findings.

Compute-aware experiments substantiate practical usefulness: for example, ViT-B with 400-epoch MaskSub obtains 84.1% at 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for a 600-epoch baseline at 26 GPU-days, and it outperforms DataAug, GradAug, and CoSub while using less training compute.

The ablations provide useful support: replacing distillation with masked-label supervision reduces the ViT-B gain from 0.6 to 0.1 points, performance is stable across 25–75% masking and several loss weights, and selected experiments include three-seed means and deviations. Pseudocode, extensive recipe tables, hardware costs, and released code further aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Materially, the originality and attribution to masking are not fully established. The approach is closely related to established weak/strong-view consistency training and self-distillation, including UDA, DataAug, and especially CoSub. Moreover, the 100-epoch ablation already improves from 77.4% to 78.4% with 0% masking, versus 79.0–79.3% with masking. Thus, a substantial portion of the short-schedule gain arises from generic two-pass/self-distillation effects; an equal-compute clean-view distillation control in the headline 400/800-epoch settings is missing.

Many reported improvements are only 0.1–0.4 points and lack uncertainty estimates. Repeated runs are supplied for selected 100/400-epoch and transfer experiments, but not for the 800-epoch large models, BEiT/CLIP fine-tuning, Swin, detection, GLUE, or CLIP pretraining. Consequently, the claim of consistent gains across every setting is stronger than the statistical evidence.

The proposed mechanism is supported only correlationally. Smaller early gradients are expected when matching uncertain soft targets, and lower soft-target loss does not by itself demonstrate better optimization. Masking is also applied to every sample, contrary to the interpretation that it is exclusively applied to samples with successful main-branch outputs. The claimed automatic, sample-wise difficulty control should therefore be qualified.

Some efficiency and generalization comparisons are confounded or incomplete. The ResNet equal-budget comparison changes both epochs and the RSB recipe (A1 versus A2), while hierarchical models incur approximately 2× training cost without a corresponding Swin equal-budget control. Raw robustness gains are not separated from improved in-distribution accuracy, and the large CLIP zero-shot gain lacks repeats, retrieval evaluation, and a matched-compute baseline.

Correctable clarity and reproducibility issues remain: the BCE form of distillation and full GLUE/CLIP-pretraining protocols are underspecified, and Table 7 labels both of its first two dataset columns as CIFAR100 even though the first is evidently CIFAR10. These do not overturn the core result but impede precise reproduction.

strengths: The proposed full-image supervised branch plus stop-gradient distillation to a masked branch is technically coherent, simple, parameter-free, and incurs no inference overhead. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-4omduc7w/call-4cbb3c3a61e044aaa4cbe9fc48bb6ec9/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The principal ImageNet evidence is convincing: at 400 epochs, MaskSub improves DeiT-III by 0.6–0.7 points across ViT-S/B/L/H, and the reported three-run results for ViT-B improve from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02. Gains remain consistent at 800 epochs.

Evaluation is unusually broad, covering multiple architectures and training regimes, fine-tuning, robustness, transfer, segmentation, detection, CLIP pretraining, and BERT. Compute-matched comparisons also generally favor MaskSub; for example, ViT-B reaches 84.1 in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7 for longer baseline training in 26 GPU-days.

The appendix provides useful ablations of distillation targets, mask ratio, loss weights, additional branches, dropout/drop-path variants, and selected random-seed variability. The pseudocode, fixed default mask ratio, detailed recipes, and released code support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Material: originality is only moderate. Equation 3 is essentially one-way consistency/self-distillation from an unmasked view to a strongly augmented masked view. The asserted distinction from UDA—“distillation loss” rather than “consistency loss”—is not substantive because the presented cross-entropy is itself a consistency objective. A controlled comparison with closely related teacher-student consistency methods under the same recipe and budget is missing.

Material: the experiments do not fully isolate masking from generic two-pass self-distillation. In Table A.7, a 0% mask already raises accuracy from the 77.4 baseline to 78.4, versus 79.2 at 50% masking. Thus, a substantial fraction of the gain exists without masking, weakening claims that masking is the central or necessary ingredient; this control is not evaluated at the main 400/800-epoch scale.

Material: uncertainty is reported selectively. The main 400-epoch and some transfer experiments have three-run statistics, but many claimed generalization results—particularly 0.1–0.4 point fine-tuning, detection, and segmentation gains, as well as GLUE, CLIP, robustness, and 800-epoch results—are single point estimates. BERT-large also regresses on three GLUE tasks, and applying MaskSub during CIFAR fine-tuning causes clear degradation, so the abstract's all-cases consistency claim is too strong.

Material: the proposed explanation is not adequately established. One short-training gradient-norm study does not demonstrate stochastic training instability or the claimed sample-wise “automatic difficulty control”; masking is applied to every sample, not exclusively to samples with successful main-branch predictions. The analysis shows improved optimization but does not establish the stated causal mechanism.

Material: several comparisons are not fully controlled. Table 6 mixes different base recipes when comparing self-distillation methods, the ResNet compute-matched study compares RSB-A1 against RSB-A2 plus MaskSub, and Table A.13 uses baseline results from the earlier DeiT-III paper rather than matched reruns. Moreover, the bibliography stops at 2023 and does not substantiate the manuscript's state-of-the-art positioning for CVPR 2025.

Presentation refinements include specifying the BCE distillation objective and branch-specific stochastic augmentations more precisely, correcting the duplicated CIFAR100 heading in Table 7, and tempering repeated claims such as “substantial advancement” and “training instability.”

strengths: The method is technically coherent and simple: a shared-weight clean branch supplies stop-gradient soft targets to a strongly masked branch, adding no inference-time parameters or cost; MAE-style token removal limits ViT training cost to about 1.5×.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad. Improvements are reported across DeiT-III training, MAE/BEiT-v2/CLIP fine-tuning, multiple ViT scales, ResNet and Swin, transfer learning, ADE20K segmentation, COCO detection, robustness benchmarks, and CLIP pretraining.

The core ImageNet evidence is consistent: DeiT-III gains 0.3–0.7 points across eight model/training-length settings. Compute-matched ViT comparisons also favor MaskSub; for example, ViT-B reaches 84.1 at 25 GPU-days versus 83.7 at 26 GPU-days for longer baseline training.

Ablations substantiate important design choices. Replacing distillation with hard-label supervision reduces the gains from 0.6–0.7 to 0.1 points, several mask ratios work similarly, and selected three-seed experiments report improvements larger than their measured variation.
Implementation details, pseudocode, extensive training recipes, hardware costs, and a code link provide a comparatively strong basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. The objective is essentially clean-to-masked consistency/self-distillation with shared weights and stop-gradient, closely related to established consistency training, self-distillation, UDA, and CoSub. Comparisons do not fully isolate it against generic clean-view self-distillation, masking curricula, or other consistency objectives under identical compute and recipes.

The claimed explanation through training “stability” is not adequately established. The paper shows smoother loss/accuracy curves and branch gradient norms for one 100-epoch ViT-B setting, but defines no stability metric, demonstrates no divergence or across-seed instability, and provides no causal test showing that the evolving soft-target difficulty explains the gains.

Statistical evidence is incomplete for the headline results. Three-run statistics cover selected ViT-B/ViT-S and transfer experiments, whereas many gains in fine-tuning, Swin, downstream tasks, and BEiT-v2 are only 0.1–0.4 points and are reported from apparently single runs.

Several comparative claims are stronger than the controls justify. The self-distillation table compares absolute accuracies obtained with different base recipes; the ResNet compute-matched comparison changes from RSB-A1 to RSB-A2 and omits the ResNet-50 case that loses 0.4 points in the appendix; and comparisons among CLIP-derived methods mix different pretraining procedures.

The transfer table lacks the full 2×2 factorial comparison—MaskSub fine-tuning is not evaluated with the ordinary pretrained model—so it cannot cleanly separate pretraining and fine-tuning effects. Minor presentation issues, such as the duplicated CIFAR-100 heading, inconsistent ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16 naming, and pervasive overstatement, should also be corrected but are not decision-determining.

strengths: The method is technically coherent and simple: a shared network learns from labeled clean inputs while matching stop-gradient predictions on a strongly masked view. It adds no parameters or inference cost, and token removal limits ViT training overhead.

The empirical breadth is unusually strong: experiments cover ImageNet training and fine-tuning, four ViT scales, ResNet, Swin, MAE/BEiT/CLIP initialization, transfer learning, segmentation, detection, robustness, BERT, and CLIP pretraining.

ImageNet gains are consistent across major settings, including +0.3 to +0.7 points for DeiT-III models. Robustness improvements are sometimes substantially larger, such as +3.5 to +6.4 points on ImageNet-A.

Compute-aware comparisons strengthen the practical case. MaskSub improves several models over longer-training baselines at comparable GPU-days and is cheaper than the evaluated two-view alternatives, although the advantage is not universal.

The paper includes useful ablations showing that distillation is essential, performance is insensitive across a broad range of masking ratios, and the default loss weighting is reasonable. Pseudocode, recipe tables, and a stated code release aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Material: conceptual originality is limited. The objective is essentially clean-to-strong-view consistency/self-distillation with masking, closely related to established weak/strong augmentation consistency and CoSub-style training. The paper discusses these connections but does not convincingly establish a fundamentally new learning principle.

Material: attribution specifically to masking is incomplete. The 0%-mask self-distillation control already improves 100-epoch accuracy from 77.4 to 78.4, while masking raises it further to about 79.2. An equal-compute clean-view distillation control under the main 400/800-epoch settings is missing.

Material: claims of training “stability” and “automatic difficulty control” exceed the evidence. Faster loss convergence and changing average gradient norms do not establish instability mitigation or the proposed sample-wise mechanism; masking is applied to every example, contrary to the statement that it is applied exclusively to successfully predicted samples.

Material: uncertainty is reported only selectively. Many headline improvements are 0.1–0.4 points and come from single long runs, while some transfer gains are smaller than the reported standard deviations. GLUE and CLIP results also lack repeated-run uncertainty, making the strongest consistency claims less secure.

Material: the added training cost remains significant—about 45% for the principal ViT setting and roughly 100% for hierarchical architectures. Compute-matched benefits are mixed: the ResNet-50 comparison loses 0.4 points and the 800-epoch ViT-S advantage is only 0.1.

Presentation: several assertions are overstated and there are minor terminology and typographical issues, but these are refinements rather than reasons for rejection. Overall, the broad and generally consistent evidence supports weak acceptance despite incremental novelty and incomplete causal validation.
