strengths: MaskSub is simple and practical: it adds no model parameters, requires only an asymmetric self-distillation loss, and reduces the masked ViT branch's cost through token removal. The equations and pseudocode make the central method easy to understand.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. Improvements are reported across DeiT-III ViT-S/B/L/H training, MAE/BEiT-v2/CLIP fine-tuning, ResNet and Swin, ADE20K, COCO, robustness benchmarks, BERT, and CLIP pretraining. The generally consistent direction of the results supports usefulness beyond one architecture or benchmark.

The paper addresses computational cost rather than comparing only equal epoch counts. For example, 400-epoch MaskSub ViT-B obtains 84.1% at 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for a 600-epoch baseline at 26 GPU-days, and MaskSub is substantially cheaper than CoSub in the reported controlled comparison.

The ablations are informative: they examine the distillation loss, mask ratio, loss weighting, multiple branches, alternative drop regularizers, and equal-budget behavior. Three-run results in Tables A.12-A.13 show gains larger than the reported variation for the tested ViT-S/B settings.
Reproducibility is supported by concise pseudocode, detailed training-recipe tables, a largely fixed 50% mask ratio, hardware/cost reporting, and a public code URL.
weaknesses: Material: the conceptual novelty is incremental relative to asymmetric consistency training and CoSub-style self-distillation. More importantly, Table A.7 shows that the 0%-mask two-pass variant already improves the 100-epoch ViT-B baseline from 77.4% to 78.4%, versus 79.2% at 50% masking. Thus, a substantial fraction of the gain may come from generic duplicated-view self-distillation or network stochasticity; this crucial control is not evaluated across the headline 400/800-epoch settings and architectures.

Material: the claimed training "stability" and automatic, sample-wise difficulty control are not conclusively demonstrated. Figures 2 and A.1 report loss and gradient trajectories but no divergence frequency, across-seed variability, target entropy, or sample-conditioned analysis. Masking is applied to every sample, so the statement that it is applied exclusively to successfully predicted images is also not literally supported.

Material: uncertainty is missing for many headline gains, including 800-epoch and large-model training, 0.1-0.4 point fine-tuning improvements, downstream detection/segmentation, GLUE, and CLIP. Table A.13 also states that the central baseline comes from the original DeiT-III paper rather than an explicitly paired rerun. This makes the smallest improvements difficult to distinguish from run-to-run or implementation variation.

Material: not all compute comparisons are controlled. The equal-budget ResNet comparison changes the recipe from RSB A1 to A2 as well as adding MaskSub, and ResNet-50 is actually 0.4 points worse. Several broader comparisons in Tables 2 and 6 mix recipes and omit comparable cost information, weakening their state-of-the-art conclusions.

Presentation/reproducibility refinements: the CLIP distillation objective and Swin mask-token implementation need more precise specification. There are also correctable inconsistencies, including the duplicated CIFAR100 heading in Table 7, ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16 naming, and the claim of a universal 50% mask ratio despite using 15% for BERT.

strengths: The method is technically coherent and simple: an unmasked supervised branch teaches a strongly masked, shared-weight branch through a stop-gradient soft target. It adds no model parameters or inference-time cost, and token removal limits ViT-B training overhead to about 45% in the reported measurements.

The evaluation is unusually broad. MaskSub improves DeiT-III across ViT-S/B/L/H and 400/800-epoch schedules, ResNet and Swin models, several pretrained-model finetuning recipes, downstream segmentation and detection, and every reported ImageNet robustness metric.

The ablations substantiate important design choices. Replacing the distillation target with labels reduces the ViT-S/B gains from 0.7/0.6 points to 0.1, while mask-ratio, loss-weight, multiple-branch, dropout, and drop-path studies further characterize the method.

Compute-matched comparisons are provided rather than relying only on equal-epoch results. The concise pseudocode, extensive recipe tables, hardware reporting, public code link, and three-seed statistics for selected experiments also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is modest. MaskSub is fundamentally clean-view-to-strong-view consistency/self-distillation, closely related to UDA-style weak/strong consistency and especially CoSub; the manuscript does not sharply establish why this is more than a useful supervised masking instantiation or compare against stronger same-recipe consistency/teacher alternatives.

The claimed mechanism is not fully established. Gradient-norm curves are compatible with increasing teacher confidence, but do not demonstrate that automatic difficulty control causes the gains. Moreover, masking is applied to every sample, so the statement that it is applied “exclusively” to successfully predicted samples is inaccurate.

Statistical evidence is incomplete for the headline breadth claim. Many improvements are only 0.1–0.4 points and lack repeated runs, including most 800-epoch, finetuning, Swin, detection, GLUE, and BEiT results; the reported three-seed experiments cover only a subset. Some individual GLUE and CIFAR transfer results also decrease, contrary to the strongest consistency language.

Several comparisons support usefulness but not the stated superiority claims: the self-distillation table confounds MaskSub with the stronger RSB recipe, and some cross-paper pretraining comparisons mix recipes and budgets. Training overhead is also material—about 45–50% for token-dropping ViTs and approximately 100% for hierarchical models—while the zero-additional-memory claim is not empirically profiled.

Presentation issues are secondary but noticeable: Table 7 labels both CIFAR columns as CIFAR100 although the first is CIFAR10, ViT-H/14 and ViT-H/16 are used inconsistently, and repeated terms such as “state-of-the-art,” “remarkable,” and “consistent across all cases” overstate portions of the evidence.

strengths: MaskSub is simple, technically coherent, and practical: the masked view learns from detached soft predictions of the unmasked view using shared parameters, while inference requires neither extra parameters nor extra computation.

The central empirical evidence is broad and consistently favorable. On ImageNet-1k, MaskSub improves DeiT-III by 0.3–0.7 points across ViT-S/B/L/H and 400/800-epoch schedules, and gains also appear for MAE, BEiTv2, and CLIP fine-tuning, ResNet, Swin, downstream recognition, segmentation, detection, and robustness benchmarks.

The paper takes computational fairness seriously. GPU-day-matched comparisons show, for example, 400-epoch MaskSub reaching 81.2/84.1 on ViT-S/B versus 80.7/83.7 for 600-epoch baselines at approximately equal cost. Token removal limits ViT training overhead to roughly 45–50%, with no inference overhead.

The ablations support the proposed design: replacing soft distillation with ground-truth supervision reduces gains from 0.6–0.7 to 0.1 points; performance is robust across 40–75% masking; and 50% masking outperforms a zero-mask two-pass self-distillation control despite using less computation. Loss-weight, branch-count, and alternative drop-regularization studies further clarify the design.

The main algorithm is clearly presented and easy to implement. Detailed training recipes, three-run statistics for selected core and transfer experiments, and an available code repository provide a reasonable foundation for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The conceptual originality is moderate. At its core, MaskSub is asymmetric weak-to-strong consistency or online self-distillation with masking, closely related to UDA-style consistency training and especially CoSub. The efficient masked-token instantiation is useful, but the manuscript's distinctions from prior frameworks rely more on application setting and stated objective than on a fundamentally different learning principle.

The claimed mechanism of “training stabilization” and “automatic difficulty control” is not established rigorously. It is inferred from loss and gradient-norm curves for one 100-epoch ViT-B setting; the gradient-norm measurement is insufficiently defined, lacks uncertainty, and does not causally distinguish the proposed explanation from ordinary regularization or curriculum effects.

Uncertainty is missing for many results whose gains are only 0.1–0.4 points, including several fine-tuning, Swin, segmentation, detection, 800-epoch, and GLUE experiments. Three-run statistics are provided only for selected settings, and the provenance of quoted versus independently rerun baselines is not always clear, weakening confidence in the smallest improvements.

The favorable 1.5× cost applies primarily to ViTs where masked tokens can be removed. ResNet, Swin, DropSub, and PathSub require about 2× training computation; moreover, the equal-budget ResNet-50 comparison is negative (80.0 versus 80.4). Thus, the practical efficiency and generality claims need qualification.

Some broad claims exceed the evidence: CLIP fine-tuning has the same best accuracy as its baseline and improves only the last-epoch value; several GLUE tasks and CIFAR fine-tuning results decline; and non-vision experiments omit important details and multi-run evidence. Minor presentation issues—including a duplicated CIFAR-100 heading, inconsistent ViT-H naming, imprecise vector notation in the losses, and several typographical errors—are readily correctable and do not determine the recommendation.

strengths: MaskSub is technically coherent and practical: it combines ordinary supervised learning on the full input with stop-gradient self-distillation on a heavily masked view, shares all parameters, and adds no inference-time cost.

The central evidence is broad and consistently favorable. On ImageNet-1k, MaskSub improves DeiT-III by 0.3–0.7 points across ViT-S/B/L/H and both 400- and 800-epoch schedules; gains also appear for ResNet, Swin, pretrained-model fine-tuning, downstream recognition, and robustness benchmarks.

The paper treats training cost seriously. For example, ViT-B MaskSub obtains 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for a longer baseline in 26 GPU-days, and it provides a better accuracy/cost trade-off than the reported DataAug, GradAug, and CoSub comparisons. MAE-style token removal makes the masked branch substantially cheaper than a second full branch.

The ablations support important design choices: replacing distillation with hard-label supervision reduces the ViT-B gain from 0.6 to 0.1 points, masking ratios from 25% to 75% work similarly, and selected core experiments include three-seed means and standard deviations.

Pseudocode, fixed default masking ratio, hardware and GPU-day accounting, detailed image-training recipes, and released code make the principal experiments reasonably reproducible. This assessment is based on the complete manuscript. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-lymescp1/call-b11e94f8125f4ce4893007fafa0b59f6/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The conceptual originality is modest: the objective is an asymmetric weak/strong-view consistency or online self-distillation loss, closely related to established consistency training and CoSub. A matched generic consistency baseline using another strong augmentation is missing. Notably, the 0%-mask condition already improves accuracy from 77.4% to 78.4%, versus 79.2% at 50% masking, showing that a substantial part of the benefit is not specific to masking.

The proposed explanation is not established by the analysis. The directly masked model converges to lower accuracy, but the presented curves do not demonstrate numerical instability. Aggregate gradient norms also do not prove the claimed sample-wise automatic curriculum: every sample is masked, and a confidently incorrect main branch can provide a strong incorrect target.

Uncertainty is reported only for selected experiments. Several results underlying the broad applicability claim are just 0.1–0.4 points—such as BEiT-v2 fine-tuning, Swin-T, and COCO detection/segmentation—without repeated-run variation, while the large-model, CLIP, robustness, and most downstream results also appear to be single runs.

Some disclosed outcomes qualify the universal claims: the best CLIP fine-tuning checkpoint is stated to equal the baseline despite a better final epoch; applying MaskSub during transfer fine-tuning hurts CIFAR performance (e.g., ViT-B CIFAR-100 falls from 91.9 to 89.6); and compute-matched ResNet-50 loses 0.4 points. These do not overturn the main findings but should be reflected more clearly in the conclusions.

The transfer experiment omits the factorial condition with ordinary pretraining followed by MaskSub fine-tuning, so pretraining and fine-tuning effects are partly confounded. The beyond-vision evidence is also less reproducible: the paper does not specify how the distillation objective handles the STS-B regression task, and GLUE seed/model-selection details and precise CLIP scheduling, compute, and data-mixture settings are incomplete.

Some cross-paper comparisons—especially the self-distillation table—mix different base recipes, so absolute accuracy does not cleanly establish method superiority. Presentation-only issues include the duplicated CIFAR-100 heading where the first column should be CIFAR-10 and inconsistent ViT-H/14 versus ViT-H/16 notation. Overall, the extensive paired evidence and practical utility outweigh these reservations, but the limited novelty and overextended mechanistic claims keep the recommendation at weak accept.

strengths: MaskSub is technically simple and practical: it combines supervised loss on an unmasked view with stop-gradient self-distillation on a strongly masked view, shares all parameters, and adds no inference-time machinery. MAE-style token removal limits ViT training cost to approximately 1.5× rather than 2×.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. DeiT-III ImageNet training improves by 0.3–0.7 points across ViT-S/B/L/H and 400/800-epoch schedules; gains also appear for MAE, BEiT-v2, and CLIP fine-tuning, ResNet and Swin training, ADE20K, COCO, robustness benchmarks, BERT, and CLIP pretraining.

Useful controls support the basic design. Replacing distillation with hard-label supervision reduces the ViT-B gain from +0.6 to +0.1; mask-ratio and loss-weight studies show reasonable robustness; and comparisons at approximately matched GPU budgets generally favor MaskSub over merely extending training.

The manuscript is clear and largely reproducible through concise pseudocode, detailed recipe tables, compute reporting, a public code link, and three-run mean/standard-deviation results for selected core and transfer experiments.
weaknesses: The masking-specific attribution remains incomplete. At 100 epochs, a zero-mask second distillation pass already improves accuracy from 77.4 to 78.4, versus 79.2 with 50% masking, while the hard-label ablation shows that distillation supplies most of the main-setting gain. A zero-mask distillation control at 400/800 epochs and matched alternative-corruption controls are absent, so the results establish the complete recipe more strongly than the claimed special role of masking.

Most small improvements lack repeated-run uncertainty: examples include BEiT-v2 (+0.1), Swin-T (+0.1), COCO (+0.2/+0.3), several fine-tuning results (+0.1–0.4), and BERT-large GLUE (+0.3 average). The selected three-seed experiments are reassuring, but they do not establish that all of the paper's claimed consistent gains exceed run-to-run variability.

Several headline comparisons are not fully controlled. The self-distillation table mixes MaskSub with a stronger RSB recipe against methods using older recipes; the pretraining table compares supervised MaskSub against label-free MAE objectives; and the equal-budget result is not universal—ResNet-50 MaskSub obtains 80.0 versus 80.4 for the longer baseline. Hierarchical models also require approximately 2× training computation. Moreover, CLIP fine-tuning reportedly has the same best-epoch result as its baseline, despite the claimed improvement based on the last epoch.

The proposed explanation is stronger than its evidence. A rising sub-branch gradient norm does not by itself demonstrate sample-wise “automatic difficulty control,” the gradient-norm measurement is not defined precisely, and masking is applied to every sample rather than “exclusively” to samples the main branch predicts successfully.

Originality is moderate: the method is principally asymmetric consistency/self-distillation between clean and corrupted views with shared weights, closely related in structure to established consistency training and CoSub-style online distillation. The masked, compute-efficient instantiation is useful, but claims of a general or substantial new training principle are overstated. Minor inconsistencies—including the duplicated CIFAR100 header and ViT-H/16 versus ViT-H/14 naming—also merit correction.
